utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. The Chamber was informed that there were a few preliminaries to be raised. Prosecution -- oh, there is a ... the transcriber is ready. Yes. I started saying that some preliminary issues were announced to be raised. Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, there are two preliminary matters and if we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform Your Honours that I did my homework, and I checked the documents introduced as associated exhibits through the Witness RM321 and we do not have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is for all ten of them, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was ten, yes. I don't have the numbers here, but I'll revisit the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- yes, here I have got it. P1790 up to and including P1799 are admitted into evidence all as public exhibits. Then before we give -- before we continue the examination of the witness, there are a few matters the Chamber would like to raise as well. The first one is about the end of the Prosecution's case. On the 9th of July of this year, the Prosecution, upon inquiry by the Chamber, provided information on the scope and schedule of presenting the remainder of its evidence. The Chamber was surprised to learn of the large amount of documents the Prosecution intends to still tender, especially given the many guidances the Chamber has provided on tendering documents through witnesses and not through bar table motions. As a result, the Chamber fixes the following schedule: All 92 bis, 92 quater, and bar table motions shall be filed by the 30th of August, 2013. The Prosecution did indicate that this was possible with the exception of one filing. That last filing can be submitted by the 16th of September, 2013. As regards the Prosecution's submission that associated exhibits tendered with pending or future 92 bis motions may be denied and would then need to be bar tabled, the Chamber reminds the Prosecution of its guidance that neither bar tabling nor tendering as associated exhibits is the preferred way of tendering. One option for such documents would be to use and tender them through witnesses coming to court. In relation to military documents as well as UN documents, the Chamber considers that the parties could agree on certain matters in a more succinct form. Further, the Chamber urges the Prosecution to carefully consider whether all documents are necessary to satisfy the Prosecution's burden of proof. In this context, the Chamber urges the Prosecution to avoid repetition, reduce the number and length of documents, and take away details not vital to the case. In addition, the Prosecution should explain how the documents fit into its case and provide an explanation why the documents could not be tendered through witnesses. Lastly, the Chamber instructs the Prosecution to batch the bar table documents in its motions into clearly defined and focused groups. The documents should be batched by topic or subject matter; for example, by crime base incident. This concludes the observations by the Chamber on the end of the Prosecution's case. There is one other matter I would like to raise because it is of some urgency. Next week the Prosecution will call expert Witness Haglund, who is a forensic anthropologist. The Prosecution tenders 15 reports through him, all in all almost 3.000 pages. The bulk of this material are, in fact, the underlying autopsy reports the witness bases his conclusions on. The Chamber reminds the Prosecution of its guidance and direction of the 29th of October, 2012, in relation to the tendering of underlying documents for expert reports. The Chamber, therefore, asks the Prosecution to reduce the material tendered for Witness Haglund and specifically to refrain from tendering Rule 65 ter numbers 4550 to 4552, 4555 to 4557, 4561 to 4562, as well as parts of 65 ter 4558. Should any of the information contained in these underlying documents not be reflected in the actual expert reports, the Prosecution is free to elicit such evidence viva voce. And this concludes the observations by the Chamber in relation to expert witness Haglund. Is the Defence ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Lawrence? Then could Mr. Lawrence be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lawrence. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lawrence, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to begin by asking you a few questions about autopsy work in general to see if we can find a common ground, and first I'd ask you if you -- if you agree with me as follows, that in a normal situation, a decision on whether an injury was sustained while the person was alive or if it's a post-mortem one is, to a large degree, based on the observation of surrounding tissue and things that can be connected with that such as bruises, swelling, and bleeding? Can we first agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Further, Doctor, can we agree that in a decomposed body in which tissue changes the colour very quickly and starts to break off, this becomes very difficult, and if the post-mortem remains are already skeletonised, then it is impossible. Before healing begins, it will look just the same as a fracture weeks before or after death. The existence of bruises is the only thing that can differentiate between such injuries?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I agree with the general proposition. There are some differences in boney injuries in bone that is moist and fresh and bone that is bare and dry. But in general I agree with your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can call up 1D1141 in e-court. And if we can have page 14 of that document which should correlate to transcript page 7527 of the Popovic proceedings. I apologise, page 20, page 20, which should be 7533 of the underlying transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Doctor, you may follow along with me. I would like to revisit a question and answer that were made beginning at line 5 onward. "Q. I would now like to put to you a hypothetical question; and since you are an expert, I believe that you will be able to answer it. If an arm belonging to a person was found in a secondary grave and in a completely different secondary grave the other arm was found belonging to the same person, in your reports, this would appear to be two persons or two bodies that were found. Is that correct? "A. Not exactly. I have given you figures on causes of death for the complete bodies and then for the incomplete bodies. I think the information on the complete bodies is fairly reliable, but it's obviously extremely difficult in an incomplete body to conclude whether or not there were one person killed or two people killed. It just wasn't possible ... if we had been able to match every one of the bodies, it may have been possible. "The reason I have included both information on the whole bodies and the body parts is, I think, in particularly some of the more disrupted graves such as Liplje, it -- it would be hard to get any useful information. I also needed to indicate, I think, how many gun-shot wounds we had. But I agree, it -- it is very difficult unless you can completely reunite all of the body parts to interpret exactly what the results on the body parts means in terms of an actual cause of death." And, first of all, sir, does this appear to accurately reflect the testimony that you recall giving?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you still stand by the same?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- in rereading it, I -- I think that I observed something -- some more information. The -- and this is slightly -- this is more in the province of the anthropologist than myself, but in the current case where you had an -- a hypothetical case, an arm from one individual in one grave and the arm from another individual in another grave. The assessment of the minimum number of individuals would probably deal with that to indicate that it was one person that -- the total numbers of people. But I agree that the -- it is -- the concept of a cause of death for a body part is difficult unless you can collect together all of those body parts, match them by DNA, and reconstruct them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now dealing specifically with the work that was done on these -- on the bodies recovered from the graves that are the subject of your report, can you tell us how many autopsies would be performed per pathologist per day on average?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- I -- in my own case, I would do about four or five a day depending on the completeness of the body. An incomplete body would take less time than a complete one, but I wouldn't imagine that many of the pathologists would be doing more than six and some would be doing as little as four.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you describe that number as being in line with the normally accepted procedure in that line of work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure there is an accepted procedure in this line of work. I thought it was important for the pathologist to perform the work thoroughly. Certainly, it could have been done faster, but I was more concerned to make the work done good than quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt. Mr. Lawrence, you are talking at page 10 in response to Mr. Ivetic's question, you said: "But in the current case we had a hypothetical case, an arm from one individual in one grave and an arm from another individual in another grave ..." But the hypothetical question put to you didn't sound to me to be talking of two individuals. The question reads: "I would now like to put to you a hypothetical question ..." And I jump onto the right place. "If an arm belonging to a person was found in a secondly grave and in a completely different secondary grave the other arm was found belonging to the same person ..." That's the hypothetical question put to you. Now, does that change your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry -- no, I'll pause. Sorry. Yes, that's what I was trying to allude to when I qualified my answer. That's one of the reasons why we did the calculations of minimum number of individuals. In that particular case, you would, say, have a right humerus in another grave and a left humerus in another grave. Now, that would be sorted out by the minimum number of individuals. That's why we used that technique to assess. But it does not solve the issue that, for example, if both of them had a gun-shot wound going through the right or left humerus close to the shoulder, looking at the body parts you might attribute a cause of death to both. I think that is why in the end I focused most of my report on the intact individuals, because there is potential for some of the data on the incomplete bodies to be slightly misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question. That would not be necessarily the case for all incomplete bodies. If, for example, you would have the upper part of a body or just a skull, then, of course, another skull would mean another person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for the arms the example is fine, but for a skull or for the complete pelvis, or there it would be different and you could count them within the number -- minimum number of bodies even if you had only found the skull.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct and that is why, when we were considering the body parts, the heads, for example, were examined by -- always examined by a pathologist because essentially if you found a gun-shot wound in the head, you could reliably assume that the individual to whom that skull belonged was dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you find bodily remains, I think, in general, even without gun-shot wounds, you can assume that that person is dead. If you would agree with me. But what you may have intended to say is that that person -- that there is a fair chance that they would have been killed by a bullet which impacted on his head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although you can't exclude other causes of death but you'd know that such an impact most likely would cause death, and then the only remaining issue is whether it was a post-mortem impact which is still an opportunity -- a possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we -- I think we agree on many parts of this part of your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in relation to the method or criteria that was utilised in doing the autopsy work in Bosnia to research, analyse, and identify victims, am I correct that that was a continuation of the criteria that had been developed by your predecessor Dr. -- I believe it was Bill or William Hunt?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can take a look at something I think relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D1141 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D4141"], page 26 in e-court, which should be transcript page 7539.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could follow along with me, sir, I would like to revisit the questions and answers from lines 5 through 21. And I begin: "Question" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you begin, I think it is 1D1141. It is not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Beginning now, sir. "Q. Thank you. Given that you answered a question of Mr. Lazarevic saying that before you went to the location, before you started working on this, you received certain instructions from the Prosecution, or rather from the investigators, could you tell us whether anybody informed you that there is such a custom in Bosnia and Herzegovina that a victim of an armed conflict is buried with a weapon? "A. No. "Q. Perhaps I was a bit imprecise. I said a victim of an armed conflict, and I wanted to say a participant of an armed conflict. I'm referring to a soldier who was killed. "A. The answer is still no. "Q. Can you then tell me why did you consider this to be a potential indicator as to whether this was a participant in an armed conflict or a victim whose cause of death could have been somewhat different? "A. Because I thought it would -- it was one criteria that might specify between them. I didn't say it was necessarily a good criteria, but it is a criteria." First of all, sir, can you confirm if this testimony from the Popovic case is accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you so testify today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in talking about a criteria in your answer, is this a criteria that you developed or would it be one that you inherited from Dr. Bill Hunt's methodology?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't recall. I know that in Bill Hunt's work, they did at least find one soldier who was carrying a hand-grenade and that may have been why he reported it. I think it was largely carrying on something that Bill did, but to be honest, it's so long ago now I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough, sir. I'd now like to look together with you at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have 1D1138 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for it, sir, I can tell you I believe it to be a publication of the Royal College of Pathologists of Australia entitled "Pathway." Are you familiar with such a publication or such an organisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see now the cover page of this document which has your picture. Do you recall, sir, having given an interview to this organisation and when that would have been published?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall doing it. I can't remember when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Would it have been before or after your work for the Office of the Prosecutor in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been after.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can go to page 2 of the document in e-court, and that is the text of the actual article, I'd like to discuss a few things with you. If we focus on the bottom of the first column and then the top of the middle column, I'd like to ask you about that, where it begins as follows: "'Where hostilities have descended into the barbarity of a massacre, the way to approach the evidence is one body at a time,' he says. "'You have to prove every single one. If they are in a mass grave, it's easy, but in places like Kosovo, where they are all buried in single graves, you have to look at each one and determine whether there is enough evidence. "'If you don't get a good nexus between your investigation and your exhumation and autopsy process, then the exhumation is useless. So it's got to be done very thoroughly and it's an incredibly expensive process.'" Now first of all, Doctor, can you confirm if this accurately recollects the statements that you would have made, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not given in a court of law, and I think it's fairly accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you say that if bodies are in a mass grave it is easy, does this mean that, as a working presumption, you as a pathologist consider that all bodies found in a same mass grave come from the same event and met their fate in the same event?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. As I've pointed out later in the article, the autopsy process is just one step of the investigation. You have an investigation, you have an exhumation, you have an examination. All of those parts are important in assessing the significance of the findings. However, as a general principle, the finding of a body that's been in one mass grave and then moved to another mass grave I think is germane to your consideration of what the cause and manner of death might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in such a process and such a consideration, does one not take into account that mass graves might arise by operation of law in a particular jurisdiction? For instance, for bodies collected in a sanitisation procedure after a battle?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask first. I -- a quote has been given to you, but I would like to first understand fully what you're quoted to have said. The first: "Where hostilities have descended into a barbarity of a massacre," that means there that you have a kind of a presumption that there is a massacre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure those words were mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- as I say, this was not prepared as a court statement. It was taken by a journalist who I think used some journalistic license in those words. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- unlikely I used those specific words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but then I'll continue. "'You have to prove every single one.'" What do you think you have to prove?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry. This was in reference to -- hold on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what makes it easy if there are in a mass grave -- to establish the cause of death? Or I would think that if you take them one by one, at least I would start thinking that it doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, this -- this was really a comparison between my experience in Bosnia and in Kosovo, and I think it relates to this issue of the step-wise process of investigation, the same investigation, the examine -- the autopsy, the exhumation and the autopsy examination. Where there was no linkage between -- where they were in separate graves and there was no apparent linkages between them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it was much more difficult to interpret the significance of the findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for you or for the Judges later or for the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- prosecutors --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you've got a large number of bodies in one place that has -- where the body has been buried and then dug up and then reburied, that would, to me, indicate that there was some intention to perhaps conceal the nature of the -- the death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now is that part of your specific expertise, whether there were -- what kind of intentions there were behind, or is it for you to describe what you see and then to leave the conclusions to those who have a total overview over the facts, perhaps over the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I accept your -- your point, there, Mr. President. I was trained in both the English and American systems. In the English system, I would give purely the cause of death. In the American system, I would be expected to give both the cause of death and the manner of death. Even in the English system, you often do consider issues like manner in relation to your cause of death. For example, the difference between a gun-shot wound that may have caused a suicide or gun-shot wound that may have caused -- may have been a homicide. So there are times in pathology when you do have to consider both cause and manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I accept that ultimately that is an issue that does not need to be resolved by me but does, as I say, need to be resolved by the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said it's easy, apparently referring to the Kosovo experience -- no, no, to the Bosnian experience. What makes it easy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I should have probably qualified that to easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't regard it as being "easy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And then what would be easy -- easier to prove?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think the fact that -- that you've got all of those bodies together indicates that -- that it relates to one event rather than several events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least there may be indications of -- of that having happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you say -- yes, so I now understand that where you are quoted to have said, "You have to look at each one and determine whether there is enough evidence," that is in the same comparison situation that to further develop thoughts on not only the cause of death but also the manner of death or any link between the several, that it's easier to develop such thoughts if the bodies are found together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I understand what the quote was about. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before I get back to the document, sir, the type of coronial system that was employed in Bosnia, correct me if I'm wrong, was the English system?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now look at the end of the middle column, the third paragraph from the bottom of this article, and it is recorded here as follows: "He might have no autopsies or up to four a day. 'Four is quite a lot. The straight-forward autopsies take about an hour. The more complicated ones can take up to four hours, so things can vary from being pretty quiet to being full-on for most of the day.'" Sir, does -- does that accurately reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was this in relation to your normal work in Tasmania or would the same observation apply to the work that was done by yourself and other pathologists in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was applied to my work in Tasmania. I still, even in Bosnia, did not often do more than four or maybe five cases in a day. But because the bodies were more decomposed, some of the dissections that I would have ordinarily undertaken in an ordinary autopsy weren't relevant. So while some of the -- some of the -- my experience in Tasmania and my experience in Bosnia are not directly comparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can move to the second-to-last paragraph on this page, that would be on the far right column, and it begins as follows: "Team-work is vital. 'You are only as good as the detectives, the crime scene investigators, the corner's officers, and the doctors involved. The autopsy is really good for checking facts, but in terms of trying to work out exactly what happened ... if you don't have enough information, you can't make an assessment.'" And can you confirm if your words are accurately reflected in this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as far as the work of the investigative team, the crime scene investigators, the detectives, those that worked on these graves in Bosnia in 1998, am I correct that you were not involved in overseeing their work or establishing protocols for their work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ivetic, could I ask similar questions as I did before. You are quoted to have said: "'You are only as good as the detectives, the crime scene investigators, the coroner's officers ...'" Do I have to understand this that you say, "The result of my work alone doesn't do the job. It is -- you need all the pieces to make my contribution a useful one"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is my view on forensic pathology that it is part of a process and that the more information that I get in regard to the circumstances, the better I can interpret what I have found. Now the trade off in that is that there is potential for bias. And one of the difficulties of being a forensic pathologist is to try and look at the material you've been given analytically and not necessarily be swayed by it but to test it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you are saying at the end if you don't have enough information you can't make an assessment. That's not very clear. An assessment about what? I take it that for the cause of death it -- you might not need all the information. And my second question would be: Were you fed with all this information -- I mean, would you have the full report of the crime scene investigators, or were you primarily doing your job by doing your autopsies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's important to recognise that this paragraph relates to my work in general and not specifically to my work in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then the question still remains: If you do an autopsy, are you asking actively for what did you find on the crime scene, or would you first do that and then make that available so that those who are overlooking the totality would be able to make a better assessment or judgement on what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I would usually try and get as much information before I started, and then look at what I found and then maybe ask for further information. So it wouldn't always be the case that I'd get all the information I wanted to start with, but it is -- it is important -- the more information I had, the more easy it was to interpret what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Such as whether a knife or a pistol was found at the crime scene, is that the kind of things you would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are things I would expect to know, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say this applies mainly for your work in Tasmania. In what way was this different than in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- well -- it's -- the nexus between the investigation and the autopsy were closer. I would normally, in a suspicious case, have attended the scene, examined the scene. I would have had all the information that -- provided by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean the scene of -- or the suspected scene of the crime --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The scene of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or the scene of where the bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The scene of the -- the scene where the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is usually -- certainly if it's a secondary grave would not be the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I was referring there in terms -- to my work in Tasmania, not the work in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now better understand. Mr. Ivetic, before we ask further questions about what the witness said, I would first like to fully understand what he is quoted to have said before asking further questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 3 of this article now, I would like to go over one more part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then have you explain it for us. And it is the far right column at the top, the first full paragraph of the same. "'In forensic, weird things tend to happen, slightly more commonly than you'd expect ... coronial cases tend to be strange and unusual. The older I get, the more careful I am never to say 'never' and never to say 'always.' I have been surprised in the past ... someone who has accidently fallen on a spike that has gone through their brain, a man driving a car where the gear stick has gone through his heart, very, very strange occurrences that you wouldn't anticipate happening but occasionally do occur. "'On a regular basis, from the history I'm given, I try to guess what the cause of death is and then do the autopsy. The only problem is it is only possible to get 60 to 70 per cent accuracy. I am nearly always surprised by what I find at autopsy. You can't even anticipate which cases you are likely to get wrong.'" Does this accurately depict your words to the journalist?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's in quotations. I think it -- I think it probably is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us then, sir, in relation -- could you explain to us what you are talking about when you say it's only possible to get 60 to 70 per cent accuracy? In relation to what, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, this is in relation to work I'm doing in -- in relation to my regular work, not in relation to what we are talking about today. But, no, what I -- what I often do is, in my cases in Tasmania, read the story, examine the outside of the body, and try and ascertain what the cause of death is before I do the autopsy, and the problem is that we know from -- from research work and so forth that the accuracy of that is about 60 to 70 per cent. You've -- you probably can't get more accurate than that. This is not really -- I -- well, I can't see the direct -- it's not meant to relate to the work we did in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could I still ask you, "It's not likely..." Do you mean that only in 60 to 70 per cent of the cases, your initial guess --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on the basis of the information provided to you and just at looking at the body from the outside that in -- in -- well, let's say 30 to 40 per cent it turns out that you were wrong in your initial guess, whereas in 60 to 70 per cent your guess was right. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I should -- this is -- I think this highlights the importance -- it was meant to highlight the importance of doing autopsies. You -- it is not meant to relate to my accuracy in terms of assessing the cause of death at the finish of the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because there you think that you can accurately establish either the cause of death or the probable cause of death or the -- well, definite cause, there you have no doubts as the accuracy of such conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We've actually done research to demonstrate this figure of 60 to 70 per cent being right. It really relates to an issue in Australian -- in Australian coronial practice where there has been a tendency to do less autopsies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this is, therefore: Is it what I thought it to be initially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at one more item for this document. If we could please scroll up to the top of this page, I think we'll see a headline, the second heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "'The high-profile cases can be quite dangerous because there is a huge amount of speculation. If you are not careful with those cases, they can go badly wrong on you.'" Do you stand by those words as being accurately published?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you still hold that view?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you consider the work that you did in 1998 for the Tribunal in Bosnia as being a high-profile case of the type that this comment was directed towards?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document as the next exhibit number at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 1D1138 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- shall be assigned Exhibit number D338. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D338 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, it may be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lawrence, we would like to see you back after the break, which will be in approximately 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic, could you give us an indication as where we are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I'm still on track to complete the witness within the estimated time that we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the estimated time was?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was two and a half hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours. Yes. Which would effectively mean what, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe just under two hours left today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One hour and 50 minutes left. 50, I should pronounce better, especially if it comes to 15 or 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Ivetic, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, yesterday you briefly told us about the Gilham case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to revisit that with the assistance of 1D1140 in e-court, which I believe is an article of the Sydney Morning Herald from 2011 about that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, sir, am I correct that you were an expert witness for the Prosecution in that case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regard myself an expert witness for the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. You were not called as a defence witness, is what I was --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In this article, if we can look at the fourth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down and to pause between question and answer so that the interpretation into B/C/S could be complete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was a firm message --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we should take to heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at the fourth paragraph from the bottom, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I can read it so that we can be on the same page. It begins: "But yesterday in the NSW Criminal Court of Appeal, Dr. Lawrence conceded that he was not fully qualified to give evidence when it came to levels of carbon monoxide below 10 per cent, and that doing so had made him 'uncomfortable.' "Dr. Lawrence said he had warned at the time that a toxicologist would be more appropriate to give evidence. He also said that he had not been given important information about Chris Gilham such as whether he was a smoker. "Dr. Lawrence said he had changed his view and believed it was possible the elder Gilham sibling was alive for at least a short time after the fire was lit." Does this accurately summarise the Gilham case that we talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a newspaper article which expresses some of the opinions of the reporter, but substantially it's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I only want to focus on the recitation that you had not been given important information, and I want to ask you: Was this information that was in the possession of a party in the proceedings? I mean, what does that part relate to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just backtrack a little. In forensics pathology, a smoker can have a carbon monoxide level of 10 or even 12, so the -- the observation of whether or not they were a smoker is relevant to the consideration, and I had not been ever informed whether or not Christopher Gilham was or was not a smoker.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was that information that had been in the possession of the police, the prosecution? Who had that information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if you know, what was the ultimate outcome of the Gilham appeal? Was the murder conviction -- or the murder convictions reversed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move on to another topic, I'd like to focus on -- upon your arrival at the Tribunal in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to recount something that's contained in 1D1141, the Popovic transcript, page 6 in e-court; transcript page 7519.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could follow along, sir, I'd like to read from line 4 through line 18, the questions and answers. "Q. Can you tell us who provided that initial briefing to you as to what had happened in Srebrenica in 1995 in the opinion of the OTP? "A. That's difficult to remember. I got information from many people, and I honestly cannot remember who told me what, but I had spoken to Graham Blewitt, John Ralston, members of the investigative team, Professor Richard Wright. So I -- I received information from a large number of people. "Q. Thank you very much. Naturally, you cannot be expected to remember every word that was uttered to you, and by whom. But could you summarise the information that was provided to you in OTP -- by OTP as to what was their impression about what had happened in Srebrenica in July of 1995? What did they tell you? "A. I -- I was told that a number of people had been killed, that they had been buried, that the graves had been then re -- dug up, and that the bodies had been reburied again." Does this accurately convey the testimony as you recall it from this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by the same?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of this transcript in e-court, I'd like to continue to see if I'm understanding this right. From line 2 I'll continue reading, sir. "Q. Thank you. When preparing to go out to work in the field, were you perhaps told that in the territory of Srebrenica municipality, as well as in neighboring municipalities of Bratunac and Zvornik, in 1992 very intense combat took place between the Serbian and Muslim forces, which is to say that this happened some three years before the 1995 event -- sorry, 1995 events. "A. Yes. I -- I was aware there had been previous combat. "Q. Was your attention drawn to the fact that in doing your work, you should bear in mind that some of the graves that you might come across were created in 1992 or 1993? Were you told to pay particular attention to that fact? "A. No. "Q. So you were never told by the Prosecution before going to Bosnia that there existed certain mass graves in the territory of Zvornik and Bratunac dating back to 1992. Did they have such information? "A. No. I don't recall being given -- told that specifically. I was aware that there were graves there, though." Does this accurately reflect the testimony that you gave in that case, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And has anything changed or would you adopt the same testimony today if asked these questions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about the combat that had occurred in July of 1995 between a mixed column of several thousand armed and unarmed Bosnian Muslim men trying to break through the Serb lines and get out of Srebrenica enclave, did your briefing from the Prosecutor's Office relay that information to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are we -- sorry, that's a question, not transcript. Sorry. Yes, I was told that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to take a look at Exhibit D329 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, sir, I can advise that this is a report of an oversight committee dated 1998. And once we look at the first page of that document when it comes up, we'll see the several persons that were members of the committee and at the bottom of the page the two Prosecution personnel, Peter McCloskey and Jan Kruszewski, who took part in the same. First of all, did either of the OTP personnel identified in this report have any role in briefing you at the time that you were working as a pathologist for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I knew both of the individuals. I would have talked to Peter about the case on a number of occasions, and I would assume -- I can't have any specific recall of talking to -- to Jan about that, but he was around at the time I was being briefed and I may well have spoken to him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Does this document appear to be something that remember having been advised of or having seen before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to page 3 of the document, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. When I read the document a bit further -- yes, I was aware of a document which was in -- related to something about San Antonio, and I believe that to be the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we can turn to page 3 of the document, I'd like to ask you about something in Roman numeral IV, and it's the last half of that paragraph, and it begins: "Even within their own country, there were differences in investigation and autopsy techniques, interpretation of findings, and differences between professional disciplines (pathology, anthropology, criminal investigatory procedure, and evidence collection). There was also a potential, if not real, conflict between the UN and PHR personnel, as well as variations on legal opinion for cause and manner of death. There was attempt to use the Minnesota Protocol, a standardised form for the autopsy recording which was developed in the early 1980s." And I'd like to ask you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all with respect to the concerns that were voiced, is this background information that would have been available to you at the time that you were briefed by the Prosecution in commencing your work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- this relates to work done in 1996. I -- I was briefed by -- about this by the South African investigator Frank, I am not sure I remember his second name. But, yes, this was discussed and I was asked to consider this in -- in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the Minnesota Protocol that was mentioned, am I correct that that is a standardised method of collecting and preserving evidence and entry of forensic findings on a written record developed by the Physicians for Human Rights group in the United States?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you and your team use the Minnesota Protocol in the work that you did in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the document -- sorry, I'll slow down. The document deals with a lot of issues in relation to torture and quite a lot of the document - which is a somewhat dated document I have to say as well - would not have been directly relevant to the -- I am familiar with the Minnesota Protocol. And when I prepared my reports, the -- the -- the pro forma documents, I considered some of the issues that were raised in the Minnesota Protocol, but I did not use that as the standard form. It just isn't relevant enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now are you familiar, then, with the Istanbul Protocol that would have been developed, I believe, in the 1990s, that specifically related to torture and cruel treatment and the types of steps that needed to be taken if opinions were to be rendered in relation to that area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, I would have to say, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can I take it then that your team did not employ the Istanbul Protocol in your work in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the next page of the document, and Roman numeral number VI, we will see a list of comments by some of the members of that mission, the 1996 mission. I'd like to highlight something that's contained in number 4 here to get your take on it, and it says, under Andrew Thomson, in the middle of his comment, it says. "Sixty-four (64) bodies removed in one day at Ovcara to spite UNTAES photographer. Not all bodies were fluoroscoped. 'Tension' between Drs. Haglund and Kirschner."' Now, as to this complaint that not all bodies were being fluoroscoped, would you agree that, if true, this would run afoul of one of the most basic first steps in the examination of human remains?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask where we're going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking your opinion about what's written in this document, sir. That's -- is fluoroscoping one of the most basic first steps in the process of --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of our major -- all of our whole bodies and major body parts were fluoroscoped in any of the cases that we thought were significant, were fluoroscoped because it is an important part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of the document, and it continues with the comments. First of all, sir, if I can focus on number 12, and Dr. Milewski, the -- a medical examiner from, I believe, the Bronx, she was a member of the team that assisted you, I believe, on three of the graves that you reported on.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here she is talking about the predecessor mission, and she complained that she was instructed how to list the cause of death by Dr. Kirschner. Was that one of the problems that you had been told about in relation to the predecessor investigations that had been performed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at number 13, we also have there Ms. Gallagher stating that Dr. Kirschner changed autopsy reports and instructed her to do so while processing the reports, "her" being Ms. Gallagher, the anthropologist. As a practitioner in the field of forensic pathology, would you agree that these charges, again if accurate, and if relating to reports of autopsies performed by other pathologists, would be a deviation from the standard of practice that is customary?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to step away from this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. I would object to this question. We don't know what we mean by the word "change" here and -- but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the question has been answered but, of course, the relevance of the answer, and, Mr. Ivetic, I think you would agree with me, very much depends on whether the substance of the report was changed or just the format or -- we do not know, at least it's not clear from here. And if you have any information about that, I think it would be worthwhile for the Chamber to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Perhaps not with this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- who might not have no personal knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you put these questions to him. And do you know exactly what changes are referred to? Apart from that you shouldn't change anything, but we easily agree on that, but do you know what kind of changes are hinted at in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my understanding, from information I was told, that the cause of death had been changed on some of the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that be detrimental for anyone who would have been suspected for having caused the death of that person? I mean, "undetermined" is relatively favourable, whereas a gun-shot wound would, perhaps for someone who would have to stand in a -- in a trial for manslaughter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And my understanding is yes, it would -- it would probably have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfavourable for anyone for having to stand trial for having played a role in the death of this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please understand, this is what would probably be regarded as hearsay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in an Australian jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were quite clear on that you have no personal observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But yes, I understand that in a number of the cases the cause of death was changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any idea about the quantity of -- of the number of reports and on what total?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- again, stepping away from the report and focusing on your work that came in 1998, in terms of the autopsies and the collection of all documentation from the autopsies, and provision of all information or documentation which would have been requested to be reviewed by pathologists performing the autopsies, am I correct that this role was undertaken by a Mr. Dean Manning and other Prosecution investigators or staff? Or if you don't recall, that's fine too. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still trying to -- I'm not sure I quite understand what you're asking there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In terms of collecting the reports or collecting artefacts that would have been recovered from the autopsy, would that work have been done by members of the Prosecution staff including a Mr. Dean Manning?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been done. I would also have viewed the reports to collect, but, yes, Dean Manning would have -- would have taken the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if a pathologist such as yourself needed some information and wanted to get some additional information relating to either the grave or anything else, would the source of that information likewise be Prosecution staff including Mr. Dean Manning?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have imagined that the primary source would be the source where you'd get that information from, the actual reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just get clarification. And this I ask from you, Mr. Ivetic. Your first question at line 11 of page 39, you said: "In terms of the autopsies and the collection of all documentation from the autopsies and provision of all information or documentation which would have been requested to be reviewed by pathologists ..." That was your question there. Now at line 20, you said: "In terms of collecting the report or collecting artefacts ..." Now, I would imagine that artefacts are -- is -- would be things that are collected around the grave, around -- and they are not necessarily documentation that would be -- that would come from autopsies. These artefacts would be items that would form the report in the autopsy if they are provided to the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that pathologists, when examining a body, photograph artefacts that would be found within the body that might not have been located at the gravesite. That was how I intended my question and I hope that's how it was received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, now I'm clearer. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to 1D1142, page 13 in e-court, which should correlate to 7382 of that underlying case. And if we could focus on the -- if we could focus on the bottom four lines and then we'll be going on the next page on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to revisit the questions and answers you had at line 22 onwards. "Q. And based on your experience, is it possible to determine the manner of death --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 22? The line 22 on my screen says: "And could you please define that for us ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see that. If we could zoom back out so that I can see which page we're on, I can direct ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 22 as we have it. Let me see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we zoom out so I could see the top of the page I can see what transcript page we're on and direct to go ... 1382, that's what we're --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: If I could assist, I believe it's the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: -- at page 7383 of the transcript, the Tolimir transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, if you can follow along from line 22 onward: "Q. And based on your experience, is it possible to determine the manner of death when the cause of death is unknown? "A. In some cases, yes, but often no. If I can give an example, one might have a, as I had in the United States, case where a person had been," if we can go to the next page, "buried in a clandestine grave and was quite badly decomposed. It was not clear exactly what had caused death, but I concluded because of the nature -- of the way the body had been concealed that the manner of death was homicide. So it is possible to have an undetermined cause of death and a determined manner of death, but it's not particularly common." Does this accurately reflect your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It relates to my general practice of forensic pathology more so than Srebrenica case, but, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the Srebrenica case, were your findings strictly related to clinically observed physical condition of remains, or did you also take into account circumstantial facts including the nature of the graves and what had been relayed to you by investigators?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered what I saw at autopsy. I considered factors like artefacts such as the ligatures and blindfolds. I think those are the -- those are the factors that I did consider in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, at this trial, protected Witness RM306 testified, and this would be at transcript pages 11472 through 11473, that per the requirements of the Yugoslavian sanitisation procedures, bodies of deceased combatants would have been buried in mass or communal graves, and that, in fact, some bodies found by the roadside were so buried in a mass or communal grave in Bratunac municipality at the Glogova site. Was such information known or conveyed to you when you were doing your work?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think I was specifically told that information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask just one more thing, RM306 also testified at transcript page 11485 through 11486 of a mass or communal grave dating from 1992 and containing 150 or 100 bodies that had been robbed in 1995 at the same time that bodies from Glogova had been removed from that site and taken away. Was such information known or conveyed to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If in relation to the diggings and the exhumations -- strike that. Am I correct that in relation to the difference between primary and secondary graves and as to which grave was a primary and secondary, you were entirely reliant upon Professor -- Dr. Richard Wright?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you at any time get information conveyed to you that the graves located along, for instance, Hodzici Road and Cancari Road were located in all instances within 5 kilometres of sites where there had been combat activity in July 1995 between the column of Bosnian Muslim males and Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could ask another question. During the whole of your work, did you find indications either in support or contradicting the option that one or more or even many of the bodies you have examined were combat casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see any case -- I -- obviously in relation to Zeleni Jadar, because of the presence of large numbers of shrapnel injuries, I considered the possibility that the -- some of these could be combat fatalities. In relation to the other sites, the presence of the blindfolds and ligatures and age -- the old age and young age of the clients, I thought that most of them -- sorry, I thought that they were probably not combatants, but I had limited information regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just asking about whether you find anything very specifically, but this is, as far as you can tell us, partly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My examination in -- the examinations that I made and observations I made seem to be consistent with the information that I was told and did not seem to contradict the information that I was told. But that's all I can really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- could I ask you the following: If you find -- if you would find a grave with a large number of people being shot in their head, entry wound at the back of the head, would you consider this to be an indication pro or contra combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if it was clear-cut that you had a single gun-shot wound in the back of the head, as some of the war crime graves in the Second World War may have shown, yes, that would be strong indication that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in your experience during your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- in this, these bodies, they were -- it was very hard to ascertain in many case the directionality of the bullets and it was not nearly as clear-cut as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just follow-up on that one, again the question was: "Would that be an indication pro or contra to combat?" And then your answer was: "It would be an indication of that --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, it would indicate to me, I think, that the person had been executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to skip ahead to another top -- to this same topic since Your Honours have raised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would like to revisit with you something from the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1D1141 in e-court, page 29 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 7542 of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And beginning at line 7 and onward, I believe, is a summary of the analysis that you performed to determine whether combatants were contained in the graves, and I would like to go through that with you to see if -- if it's complete. From line 7: "Q. Doctor, earlier this afternoon, when you were asked by my learned friend Mr. Lazarevic, on page 78 and 79, he asked you, just so we can put it in context, 'Do you believe that finding weapons in mass grave and finding bodies dressed in uniforms is important in order to establish whether the deceased was a civilian or a military serviceman?' And your answer, which appears on line 4 of page 79, is, 'It's one of the points of evidence which might answer that question.' "Do you remember that generally?"

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript says also "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I realise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then the question was posed: "What other points my help us answer that question?" And now I would like to read your answer in it's entirety and then ask you some follow-up questions. "A. I -- I think the circumstances -- I find it difficult to believe that people who are blindfolded and have their hands tied behind their backs are probably combatants at the time that they are in fact killed. I guess the other things are the general patterns of injuries that you expect to see. In modern combat, one would normally expect to see a lot of the casualties come from shrapnel, explosive devices. "It verifies from conflict to conflict, but you would expect the majority of people to have shrapnel injuries in a conflict, not gun-shot wounds, so the high -- the high number of gun-shot wounds would be odd in those circumstances. "The other thing that, frankly, I found odd was that, and this applies in forensic pathology generally, when you found that somebody has gone to some effort to conceal the body, particularly to bury them and rebury them, it's usually an indication that they're trying conceal a death. And I don't understand why someone would go to so much trouble if these were just armed conflict deaths." First of all, sir, does this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where it reads "verifies," may I take it, that's at the previous page, that you may have said "varies."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's hereby clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with that clarification, does this significantly convey the testimony that you would convey as to this question if you were asked it today?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so in this instance, the circumstantial factors or information relating to the locations of the graves and the information that you receive from the Office of the Prosecutor as to their reburial did play a role in the conclusions and the determinations that you reached in your forensic role?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, Mr. Ivetic, before the witness answers the question. Conclusions. The whole questions are focused on making a distinction between combatants and noncombatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore the question would be whether on this basis the witness has concluded that some of the bodies he performed an autopsy upon, that he defined them as combatants or noncombatants. Is that what you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Uh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the witness is asked to develop all kind of thoughts --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in which he seems not to be an expert. And then you say: Therefore this has influenced your conclusions. Now, since the questioning is about the distinction between combatants and noncombatants, my first question is whether the conclusions are distinguishing between combatants and noncombatants, because then I can see the link. Otherwise, it's just, if I could say, informed thoughts or -- well, whatever you would qualify it as. Could you please phrase your question in such a way that it's clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- also in view in matters I raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of your work, did you come to a conclusion that these bodies could be -- that you examined, excluded as combatants and combatant fatalities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think that there were some cases where I thought it was extremely unlikely that they were combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask, Doctor, was that part of your brief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you have to make those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought it was relevant in considering the circumstances, yes. I can't specifically recall if I was asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But would it be relevant to your -- the expertise that you were asked to provide to make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I provided the information that I thought might be useful in resolving the issue. Obviously, the ultimate issue goes to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. As I understand, the expert -- your expertise, and as I understand what I thought you were asked to do by those who gave you a brief, was to determine the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now was determining the status of the deceased part of your brief? That's my question. Whether it's a civilian or combatant, was that part of your brief and did you make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the answer is that in some of the cases I -- where I observed evidence that to me suggested that they weren't combatants, I included that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you perfectly, Doctor. That's your observation. My question is: Were you asked to make that determination by those who instructed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my question. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my next question would be: Did you do that? Because I looked at your first answer. You said: "I think that there were some cases where I thought it was extremely unlikely that they were combatants." Did you put -- did you write it down in your report? Did you share your thoughts with anyone, and if so, in what way? And of course in this respect only. Did you draw the attention to the fact that they were blindfolded or did you say that they were blindfolded and therefore they were not combatants? Ms. Lee, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours. The witness has answered on page 49 at line 21: "I observed the evidence to me suggested that they weren't combatants. And I included that information ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now let me -- one second. One second. "I included that information" makes unclear, and that's what I was asking, what -- whether it was written down in the report, and if so, what was written down, because "I included the information" is a rather vague notice, and therefore I asked the witness whether what he included in the report, what he observed he thought to be indicative for, perhaps, the status of the deceased person, and -- or whether he also included any conclusions on basis of that in his report in writing. That is what I -- and that's not answered by what I read in line 21 and following. Could you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I expressed an -- I wouldn't -- I expressed an opinion on some of the cases that I thought it was unlikely that these were combatants. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you then refer to any evidence you observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the things like the ligatures, the -- or, for example, the -- the injured person who then had a ligature applied to him and was then shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I expressed -- I -- it was my -- it was an observation that I made that led me to include that the person was probably not. Now, I guess it comes down to my level of certainty on that. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
