utterances.text: Well, perhaps not. Perhaps it comes down to what you were asked to do and what you did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rather than the level of certainty. But you are entering a new -- into this matter, and we leave it to Mr. Ivetic whether he wants you to do that, yes or no. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I believe you indicated that with some of the bodies the determination or your determination that they would not have been combatants was based upon their advanced age or physiological conditions or infirmaries [sic]. Am I correct that this conclusion would be based on your understanding of conventional armies such as the Australian or United States models?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have in mind or any information about the conscript armies and the Law of Total People's Defence in the former Yugoslavia that envisioned all persons between the ages of 15 and 65 to be part of the Territorial Defence forces?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You answered one of the previous questions with "yes," but I am afraid I do not fully understand what you answered "yes" to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I understood the question to be do I think that the body -- that the person who I saw the body of would have been a member of the -- a conventional army in Australia or the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what the question was. The question is about your determination that they would not have been combatants, was that based upon the advanced age, I think you answered that question earlier, physiological conditions or in ... Mr. Ivetic, could you help us, the transcript is not complete there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Infirmaries, infirmaries, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Infirmaries. And then the question is: Am I correct that this understanding would have been based of your understanding of the conventional armies such as the Australian and United States models. Now, do I understand that you wanted to ask, at least that's -- whether, if you say, older people or infirm people, that you would think of normal armies?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a simple question. It's -- it took me five times to read it. Yes. And, Mr. Ivetic, just for my understanding, the witness mentioned other factors as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are not included in this question, such as ligatures or blindfolds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm going through each one. I don't want to do a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then try to put the questions such that I even understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've had evidence at this trial of the Bosnian Muslim column being comprised of both persons armed and those unarmed, arranged by Territorial Defence brigades for purposes of their trek towards Muslim-held territory. Was that kind of information available to you at the time that you were reaching your conclusions as to whether or not these bodies could be excluded as having been combatant fatalities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe in your reports you talk about the lack of uniforms present on the remains except for an odd occasion or two where there was a military jacket, I believe, as another reason that you ruled out the likelihood of combatant casualties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would this also be rooted in your understanding of a traditional and professional army like in Australia or the United States?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We've had evidence that the Bosnian Muslim column did not have proper uniforms and that, in fact, civilians were mixed with soldiers. Did you have such information or did you consider such information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information. I did consider the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I can revisit some information that you did have, 1D1144. Page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to that one, I just wanted to find out as an addition to the list of questions we've just been putting to the witnesses, did you by any chance receive information that some of this -- these battle areas were also heavily mined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my experiences in Bosnia, I would have assumed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ivetic. It's okay, Your Honour. If we can turn to 1D1144, and page 49 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can follow along with me. I'm interested at lines -- lines 11 through 16. And the questions and answers recorded there as follows: "Q. Yes, there it is. Were you told -- was there a suggestion made to you that all these individuals were prisoners or people captured who were executed in the month of July of 1995, or were you also given a possibility that these were grave-sites dating back to various periods and various seasons? "A. No, I was told that there were prisoners who were executed." First of all, sir, is this answer accurate as to your knowledge of what you were told?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phrasing of it may not have been how I was told it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again here try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Karadzic has put a question to you which is a question which gives two options, whereas there may have been five or ten options possible. It's more or less hidden in this question. The question was were you told: "Were you told -- was there a suggestion made to you that all these individuals were prisoners or people captured who were executed in the month of July 1995, or were you also given a possibility that these were grave-sites dating back to various periods and various seasons?" That is, were they all prisoners or were these grave-sites dating back to various periods and various seasons. Now, when you said, "I was told there were prisoners who were executed," did you -- is that to be understood as that you were told that all these individuals were prisoners or people captured who were executed? Or was it that there were such among them? The question is problematic and therefore I'm analysing the question before I ask you to confirm or comment on the answer you gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I'm trying to recall something that I did 15 years ago. I can't specifically recall whether it -- which of those I was -- I mean I -- I was given information to suggest that these were -- that these were prisoners who had been executed. Whether I was given information about -- that they could have been an admixture of other cases, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you just told us that in your findings it came to your mind that those who had injuries caused by shrapnel, that you would consider them perhaps likely not to be prisoners but combat casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, and again I'm trying, you know, it's -- I'm trying to recall what my processes are, having been through court three or four times now. I think if you were to ask me, I would be -- I regarded Zeleni Jadar as being a different sort of grave and in that I would have had to consider the possibility that some of the shrapnel injury fatalities could actually be combatants. But I -- I can't, from looking at the injuries, say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Ivetic, just for my understanding. I take it that you put these questions in an effort to establish whether the witness worked on assumption that these were all prisoners. Now, that's a very direct question. I think it's about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you perform your duties and did you -- and were you led, in whatever way, in your work by the assumption that all or most of these persons were persons captured and then executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's -- that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be the issue, Mr. Ivetic, you would like to establish. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we are past the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ivetic. We will take a break, but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon Your Honours, everyone. Just briefly, Mr. President, at the conclusion of the testimony of this witness, we would ask to be able to address an evidentiary issue that arose in relation to another witness, RM506. We've been in contact with the Defence regarding this matter, and we believe we will be able to have sufficient time at the conclusion of this witness's testimony to address the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can briefly look at 65 ter number 4579, which I believe is relating to the Cancari Road 3 site. And if we could have page 19 of this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is Exhibit P1808. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the top paragraph on this page, sir, the description of the remains indicates as follows: "Many of the bodies were wearing 2 or 3 layers of clothing, e.g. trousers, long underwear, and shorts." First of all, the reference to shorts, am I correct in understanding that to be undergarments, underwear?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to what the temperatures were like in July of 1995 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider as part of your analysis or review whether this area of clothing would have been unusual relative to the summertime in that region?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it -- sorry. I did not consider that the -- the clothing to be an indication of the time of year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you consider or revise your working assumption as to the source of the bodies to take into account the possibility that some of the bodies so attired may date from another incident or another time, perhaps fall or winter in the years prior to 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ivetic. I'm not understanding your question. "Did you consider or revise your working assumption as to the source of the bodies ...?" What did you mean by "source of the bodies"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you intend to refer to people being imprisoned being executed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, yes, that's the simple way of dealing with it. So the question now is whether you considered or you revised your working assumption - and I have a question about that - as to whether these were people detained and executed, taking into account the possibility that some of the bodies so attired may date from another incident or other time, fall, winter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I still don't understand the question. It's too long and compound. I'm not sure what it seeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I rephrase it then in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- my own words and see whether -- you, when working, you assumed, on the basis of what you had heard, that the persons were captured and executed. Now, did the fact that they were dressed as they are reported to have dressed bring to your mind as an option that they may have died in a different season, a season where it is colder than July? Mr. Ivetic, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in the original question I said I would have another question on that working assumption. I heard you say that when working, you assumed that that information was accurate. Now, in what way did that -- or at least that you -- you said you assumed that it was rather prisoners executed than the other group referred to by Mr. Karadzic. Now, in what way did this acceptance of such an assumption, did that in any way influence your work and your findings? And if so, to what extent? How?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the dangers of getting any information is that it may bias your interpretation of what you do, and I am fully aware of the risks of that and try and avoid it. I think I said earlier in -- in my -- in my testimonies at some point it is partly my job to test the information I've been given to see if it matches what I've observed. A lot of the bodies that I observed were wearing multiple layers of clothing, and I assumed that that was probably because they had been displaced from somewhere and were carrying most of their clothing on them. It did not occur to me at the time that it indicated that the -- the deaths had occurred at a different time of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's not a full answer to my question. My question was also in what way the assumptions based on information you had received influenced the way in which you worked; that is, in which you performed your autopsies and drew conclusions from your findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The autopsies were carried out as we would normally carry them out. I don't think they were influenced by the information I'd been provided. The information that I provided in my reports included material that I thought needed to be highlighted as it may be significant in subsequent court considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But separate from the strict findings of you as someone who performed the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. The observations were the observations. They are -- they were not biased by -- I believe, not biassed by what I'd been told. My decision to -- in -- include information that I thought might be relevant was done so for somebody to subsequently look at and reach a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one additional question. You told us that receiving information carries a risk of bias. Does not receiving information also carry a risk of missing relevant points? It came to my mind that you said in this case where you had to review your findings that you did not receive the information that the person was a smoker. I'm thinking about whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- comparing receiving information and not receiving information as an element which may influence the accuracy of the findings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There are risks associated with not having any information, there are risks associated with having the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just follow-up. Is -- does that risk relate to the 60 to 70 per cent determination that you make by visual observation and information received, or does it also impact on the clinical autopsy that you carry out? Or is it the other way around, that the clinical autopsy may either confirm or disprove the information received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the second. It -- look, this is a complex issue, and I think the 60 per cent figure may have, I think, created a wrong impression. What I'm saying is that you -- on information in external looking at the body, you can reach some conclusions but it's not particularly accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's definitive, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's better to have all the information and do the -- the exact information, but the information can still bias your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In what way if -- I would have thought that the autopsy would be a scientific exercise that would come out irrespective of what information one had received? Put it this way: If I make a determination after an autopsy that person died because of a stab wound, and I can see the scar there, how does that -- how can that be influenced by any information I've received about the behaviour of this person before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think what it -- in a straight-forward case it doesn't, but the interpretation of a more complex injury could potentially be biased by -- by knowledge. I'm not saying a straight-forward -- gun-shot wound, there would be no question. But, for example, in a case where you had a possible gun-shot wound, the information could potentially bias your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can just follow-up on what Judge Moloto asked: Would a situation where most of the soft tissue is gone and the remains are mostly skeletonised also be a situation where there might be more cause for interpretation of physical condition or physical injuries that were reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say that the interpretation of a skeletonised body may be more subjective than the examination of a full body.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now the report we are looking at on the screen is for Cancari 3. Would you agree with me that the either grave-sites exhibited the same phenomena of persons wearing several layers of clothing and, if so, would that be noted in all of the reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think -- I think that was -- I think that phrase was standard in all the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to another criteria that you listed that we haven't gotten to, the blindfolds and the ligatures as a criteria used to exclude someone as being a combatant and to confirm the working hypothesis that they were prisoners that were executed. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is it that the witness says "on that basis I exclude"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we started off with a quotation from the Popovic case, transcript page 2542, page 29 of 1D1141, where there was the discussion of that, I believe. But I'm just trying to find it right now. Maybe it's better just to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, was the presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- of ligatures and blindfolds something else that you considered to exclude whether the remains was a combatant and to reinforce the assumption that they were a prisoner that had been executed as you had been told by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I think it -- my -- my personal opinion was that it was unlikely that a person who was -- who died with a ligature on was a combatant at the time they died.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so that would only apply to persons who actually had -- to remains, pardon me, that had a ligature attached to them --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's -- sorry, that's the only -- that would be the only cases that I was specifically referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that where such a body or such remains, if it's not a complete body, were located in a mass grave with others that did not have evidence of ligatures or blindfolds, that the same conclusions could not be imputed to those remaining bodies or remains that did not have ligatures or blindfolds?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I could not make any comment about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I go back to my earlier question: You did not make any reports about the status of the people, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, sir, that out of the 883 total bodies that are the subject of your report, there are only 83 suspected ligatures found in these same graves and that not all were affixed or attached to a body somewhere, just unknotted cloth found in the grave?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I -- I did say that there were only 53 definitive ligatures where they were ligatures that were in the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 83 pieces of cloth that I considered to be potential ligatures, but only 53 were found in a position that I thought indicated that they definitely were ligatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the same question now in relation to blindfolds. Am I correct that there were 103 suspected blindfolds recovered but only a portion of those were actually situated or affixed to a body in a place for you to conclude they were blindfolds?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Similarly, there -- 44 were in positions that led me to conclude that they were blindfolds, but there were 103 that were of a similar configuration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In the course of doing your work, can I take it that you did not access to any military records of casualties that would have predated July of 1995 from the armija BiH side in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I also correct that at the time that you were doing your work, while you took DNA samples from the remains, the results of the DNA testing were not yet known to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would like to call up 1D1148 but not broadcast the same because it does have some identifications from ICMP that I believe are not to be the subject of disclosure. Whoops. 11 -- pardon me. 1153. 1D1153. But not broadcast the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document used and admitted into evidence in the Popovic trial. It is a -- produced by a demographic expert, Ms. Svetlana Radovanovic and this list, part in English, part in B/C/S, is based on material received from the BiH Ministry of Defence by the Prosecution as to records of its soldier casualties from Srebrenica. And just so we can all follow, I would like to read so that the English translation of the headings on the left are clear. On the left side we have first a main heading that in B/C/S says: "Spisak tuzilastva," "spisak tuzilastva."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it has been pronounced by you as part of the English transcript, although in a different language. Do you have any suggestion of what it could mean Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could do that. "Spisak tuzilastva," I believe means --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: List of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then the five sub-columns are "prezime" which would be last name, "ime" which would be name, "ime oca" which would be father's name, "datum rodjenja" which would be date of birth, "datum smrti Brunborg" which would be date of death according to Brunborg. And then in the middle we have two columns with the heading "Spisak Armije BiH," "list of the Army of BiH," and two sub-columns "datum rodjenja," date of birth, and "datum smrti," date of death. And then I think the rest of the -- yes, the rest is in English on the columns so that we can understand what this is. Now, I have highlighted on the first page the one set of remains that were identified from Zeleni Jadar by DNA testing to be the individual who is named and who, according to the records of the BiH, was a casualty in either October 1994 or January 1994 depending on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee is on her feet. Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just in relation to this document itself, I just wanted to point out that this was a Prosecution document and the information contained on the left side, the Prosecution list from ABiH, that formed part of the annex of a Defence expert report in the Popovic case. However, the information contained on the right, ICMP information, was not included in that expert report, and I just wanted to have a clarification on the document itself before the -- before the witness testifies on it, just so that the witness has the relevant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It very much depends on whether the questions are about that. We do not know yet. I think it would have been wiser to wait for a second and see whether that portion of the document came into play, yes or no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, the date for this one individual whom I have highlighted is listed as 10-01-1994, which probably means January 10th but could also mean October the 1st, so I'm not going to make a conclusion one way or another. But would -- would this information cause you to feel uncomfortable with the working assumption or presumption that the bodies in, at least Zeleni Jadar, were prisoners who were executed in July of 1995 or that all the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And before the witness can answer, the information contained on the left side -- the information coming from the ABiH, those -- the facts contained in that chart had been contested and they were contested to have been inaccurate. And so it's just having -- it may be misinterpreted or misrepresenting the facts if we put the -- if we put it to the witness that these are the actual facts of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's keep matters simple. For you as well, Mr. Ivetic, but also for you, Ms. Lee. What you apparently want to ask the witness, whether if he would have known that a list existed in which the various sources give different date of death, one source considerably before July 1995 in most cases, and if that list would consist of - let me make an estimate - 120 people, I see there are four pages, whether that inconsistency would have made the witness uncomfortable in the assumption he had in his mind when he performed his autopsies. That's apparently, what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, please be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a good question as well, so we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Could you please answer that question, that with knowledge of the existence of lists of discrepancies in the dates on which [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First let -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was clear enough. Though I have not ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, let me say I haven't seen this document and I have no idea about its accuracy or anything. But if I had been provided a list that was reliable that indicated that they were -- that this person may have died at a different time, yes, I would have considered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if this information contained on this list is verified as to the one individual from Zeleni Jadar, and I can tell you there's three other individuals listed from Zeleni Jadar 5, if it is verified as to those individuals, would that give you cause to rethink whether all of the bodies in that grave-site could be linked to executions in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already indicated to you that Zeleni Jadar was a different grave to the others and that there were a lot of shrapnel -- there were a lot more shrapnel injuries and that I would consider the possibility in Zeleni Jadar that some of the fatalities were combat fatalities based on the presence of the shrapnel injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask you one question: You are talking about three which were verified. Has an attempt been made for the others to be verified and what's the result of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If that's how it came into the transcript, I apologise. I was asking if these come to be verified. Not that they have been verified, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's a hypothetical --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And if we could turn to page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, here I have also highlighted others that again, according to this information which has not been verified, were identified by DNA as being remains located in the Cancari Road 3, Hodzici Road 4, Hodzici Road 5, and Liplje 2 sites that you worked on. For each of these, again, if you are able to subsequently verify that this information as reflected in this chart is accurate as to their dates of death being in the years prior to 1995, would that give you cause to reconsider and step away from the assumption that all the bodies in those graves would have come from the same -- from the same event in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I'm sorry. I'm being asked to examine a document I've never seen before and asked a whole series of questions on it. I think it's a little bit unfair. I don't -- I don't know what this document really represents and I haven't seen it. If it's -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters simple, again. What Mr. Ivetic is asking you, that if information not yet verified would be verified, that these people died at a different date, or at least at a different period in time, whether you would change for those persons your assumption that they died in Srebrenica as prisoners and being executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah -- in the hypothetical situation that that proved to be case, yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, exactly where these people died and how they died, to what extent we find details of that in your report, I mean, would it have had an impact on the outcome? You find a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- skeletonised body, would you -- are your conclusions this was 15th July, 1995, or would you say -- yes, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to point out that Dr. Lawrence does not deal with time of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's exactly --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: -- so it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to answer the question for the witness, Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need to that. There is, of course, a strong suggestion in the questions that if you would have known that people did not die in July, would you have taken a different assumption? Now, I would say it seems to me that if the assumption is people die in July and if it's proven that they did not die in July, you have to review that they died in July. If it's not "yes," then it's -- it isn't as you thought it was. That --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- seems to be the simple matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Remember this report was prepared at the end of -- in 1999. If I was given further information that was verified, yes, I would change my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- but to what extent in your report -- or at least in the individual cases, because we are not talking about all, we are talking about a list of -- Mr. Ivetic, you may have counted them, but I came to approximately 100 or 120, approximately 30 a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And 15 of which were from the sites --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that this witness dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that have changed your findings as to the cause of death for the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would the -- again in the hypothetical, if these dates of death are confirmed for these identified remains, would the presence of those bodies in those graves also affect the working assumptions or conclusions that would have been in place when doing the autopsies and performing the reviews for all the other bodies that had as of yet been unidentified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I have to establish that you are doing again what I -- where I earlier intervened; that is, to make a kind of an implicit assumption, that what you call the working assumption was directly related to the outcome of the autopsy findings where the witness told us -- where the witness told us that the working assumption may have led to incidental observations which he thought to be relevant and not directly related to the establishment of the cause of death, if I understood your testimony well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is not the way you put it to the witness. And you may again ask a question about this subject but then in an appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When looking at the physical damage apparent on the remains as part of your forensic review, if you're work -- if your working assumption doesn't have all the information, might it cause a bias in terms of how you interpret the physical condition of the remains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please phrase a question which is understandable for normal persons as this Court. It's a lot of words, a lot of no coherence. Please put clear questions to the witness. Even if the witness understands the question, the Chamber does not as you phrased it a second ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will try to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- if the information that you received that was the basis of your working assumption could, as you testified, create a bias, is it possible for that bias to affect your physical review of the remains such that qualification of the injuries or damage to the remains would be qualified as "gun-shot wound" or "probable gun-shot wound" as opposed to some other form of injury?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That question has been asked and answered, Mr. Ivetic. I put the question to the witness and he said no. Of course, not in the -- in the words that you are using, in a much simpler way I asked him if those assumptions, the information he receives, does it impact his clinical autopsy that he undertakes, and he said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind, let's try to do it. The witness also said that information carries a risk of bias such as a lack of information may carry a risk of bias as well. On the basis of the information you received, would you consider the risk of bias to include the possibility that a gun-shot wound rather than a probable gun-shot wound would be the conclusion? I'm exploring the range of the impact of this risk of bias.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I've -- to be honest, I think that irrespective of the information I was provided, the definite gun-shot wounds would be the same. It is possible that in things like possible gun-shot wounds, the information could bias it, but I don't think it would significantly bias the definite gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say "could bias," then to become probable gun-shot wounds? Possible to probable? Is that in the range of where the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you do not exclude for the possibility that that risk of bias would result in moving from one category to another, although you almost for certain exclude that you would move into the category of definite gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, I can't say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think for the moment we've gone as far as we can with this document. Again, we'll have to check to see whether the date that is recorded as coming from the Army of BiH is accurate and I accept that we will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to move on, then, to another topic, disarticulation of bodies. There has been suggestions that the disarticulation of bodies, and by that I mean in layman's terms the dismemberment of bones from the main body, was the result of the reburial process. Am I also correct that disarticulation also occurs as part of the decomposition process as the flesh degrades and melts away from the -- from the -- from the body as well as the sinews and the muscles degrading?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The two processes, the separation of limbs and the loss of the soft tissue, the ligaments in the joints tend to hold together slightly longer than the tissue. So one would normally get decomposition and then disarticulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in the cases of bodies that have been left out in the open for some time, let's say in a battle-field, that only come to be collected at some later point in time, weeks, months, or years later when decomposition has already begun, would there be a possibility for those parts to disarticulate at the time when those bodies are lifted or cleared to be --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we've had some evidence that the column of Bosnian Muslim men was subjected to minefields, as Judge Moloto has pointed out, and also that there was the use of heavy calibre machine-guns, including anti-aircraft guns, shooting at the column. Would such heavy weapons be another potential cause for disarticulation of bodies?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, unless the rounds were buried with the bodies and recovered during the autopsy, you would not have the information available to either exclude or include that as the potential injury; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were making -- we were examining carefully for shrapnel as opposed to -- sorry, or pieces of larger weapons rather than small arms, rifles. And I would -- we did find a number of cases and I would assume we would find it if -- if there was parts of, say, for example, shells as opposed to bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But what about heavy calibre shells? Pardon me, heavy calibre bullets of machine-guns? Would they not pass through the body in all likelihood?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, again we're getting into areas that I'm not an expert on in terms of military ordinance and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question may be very relevant. Is there -- where would the Chamber have to look in order to find information about the ammunition found near or close to bodies? Because we know about bullets but my recollection doesn't serve me well to know whether there was any heavy machine ammunition found? I'm addressing both parties at this moment, Witness. Unless you would know something about it then -- Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, those issues are -- are found in the testimony of other experts. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still to come?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Well, it was contained in Mr. Manning's reports, Jean-Rene Ruez, and anthropologists's reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I may have -- my recollection doesn't serve me sufficiently. But if the witness would know anything about it, of course, he can tell us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The witness's report mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are -- as I say, I am not an expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- on ballistics, but I have attempted to describe what we found. I did not identify anything. Sorry, most of the -- most of the bullets that we found appeared to be standard small arms fire. I did not find any evidence of larger ordinance except in the cases that had shrapnel injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct, sir, that you did not recover all the projectiles from the bodies that would account for all of the holes that were in the clothing related to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In some cases the -- the projectiles had passed through the body and we did not recover them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in that instance, the calibre of those projectiles that were unrecovered would be unknown?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be unknown also even by looking at the hole? At least as a distinction between small arms and heavy arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a general concept in forensic pathology, it is not a very good idea to try and estimate the size of the bullet from the size of the hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, switching gears, am I correct that you have a working knowledge of forensic entomology? Entomology being the study of insect evidence in forensics.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I'm again a forensic pathologist. I've used forensic entomology on occasions. I would not claim to be an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of things like pupal cases or other entomological evidence in the remains that you looked at that would be of assistance in assessing the time of death?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The short answer to that is no. In Cancari Road 12 we did find some small maggots, but I suspect that they are a consequence of re-infestation of the body once they'd been exhumed and that they would not be of any use in assessing time since death.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if bodies were in the ground for several years, would you expect such entomological evidence to even still be there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I would next like to return briefly to the topic of blindfolds and ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can call up 1D1145 in e-court. And in e-court we have a surrogate sheet for the video that was given in full to the Prosecution, and then we have some photo stills from that video. I am only concerned with the photo stills, but I did want to provide the source of the photos. So if we can turn to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's 1D?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1145. So if we can turn to the part in e-court that is the stills, and if we can have page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, these are stills from a video of some combatants from the time-period, and you'll see that the soldier on the right appears to have a pink ribbon affixed to his left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to the third page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have here a soldier with a bandana, and then next to the -- what is an Army of BiH emblem, we also appear to have a pink cloth affixed to his uniform. Did you have information provided to you at the time that you were doing your review that soldiers in the region would affix coloured cloth to themselves as means of identifying friendly forces.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, how do we identify this man as a BiH soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The patch on the uniform, Your Honours, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I see -- I see the patch, but I don't see anything that says what army he belongs to. And of course, I don't know the BiH patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I apologise. It appears to be a blue shield with a white line going through it and there would be lilies. It's the -- it's the -- I believe that's the emblem of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's what you are testifying to. But I'm saying from looking at this, I want you to tell me how I must identify this as a BiH uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or in the alternative, perhaps whether the parties agree on it? The parties do not agree on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mladic. Switch off your microphone, that's one. Second -- Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The -- the agreement on the emblem itself, I mean, there is no issue with that. The only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So apparently this emblem, whether worn by whomever, but the emblem indicates that -- is the BH Army emblem?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: We have -- we have not specifically looked at the emblem itself, so that's something that we could discuss later on. At this moment, there is no agreement on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: But the question itself is irrelevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we asked you whether there was agreement --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's what I -- I tried to shorten matters, but I failed to achieve that. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the manner in which this individual in the uniform is wearing the bandana on his head, and we see he has hair, he has a certain amount of body fat, skin, if an individual wearing a bandana in this manner becomes deceased, would you agree with me once decomposition begins, the hair, skin, body fat begins to dissolve, would not this bandana slide potentially downward and cover the eyes on the skull?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But aren't we talking about facts of common knowledge? I -- I've seen many people outside any army situation, if you fall, it can slip without even being dead. I mean, let's keep matters simple. Ms. Lee -- or would you say that it's impossible that either before death or after death this bandana would slip into a slightly different position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- I mean, I would consider it almost a matter of common knowledge which, as we all know, doesn't need any proof. Yes, but I first had a question to Ms. Lee whether she would dispute that --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The question -- the possibility, no, but I would -- that is a question that should be put to the witness and not me. The possibility itself we're not disputing that. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then there is no dispute about the possibility that this may have happened. Whether it happened, the witness said he couldn't tell us. And, of course, this person, very specific, at least I do not know of him having died so that whatever may --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have happened, we -- it's just guessing and it is speculation and let's stay away from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. The hypothetical question put to you, Mr. Lawrence, by Mr. Ivetic was that it would fall down to his face. The question is: So there is something that blocks it from going down to the chin, down to the neck? It would just stop at the face? That was the underlying assumption of that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. The ears. But isn't that just general knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it general knowledge that it will stop at the eyes? Or that it could slip down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think you missed the answer. The answer was that the ears may have blocked it falling down too much further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have I understood your answer to be that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we are at the time for the break. I might have just two minutes or three minutes of questions after. If I reconstruct my questions during break, I am sure I could finish within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll give you an opportunity to do that. Ms. Lee, any estimate yet about the time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Five to ten minutes. It's going to be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we wait for the witness, I have, during the break, disassociated the video stills from the video, as I was told that that would be a complication in e-court. So the now the video stills we're looking at are 65 ter number 1D1154 and that change is put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that there is no objection against admission, Ms. Lee?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I have -- I -- Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to shorten matters, we -- we assumed that you wanted to tender it, because otherwise it would not have made much sense to separate them from the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are correct. I do want to tender it. I have not yet tendered it, but I do give notice of wanting to tender it now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I took that Ms. Lee would have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: No Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit number D339. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please be seated, Mr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more item from this stills exhibit. If I could have page 7 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in page 7 you will note that there is a strip of, again, it looks like pink cloth hanging from the medic's shoulder, and if we go to the next page, I think we'll see is a similar pink strip again on the shoulder of the wounded soldier. With respect to those suspected blindfolds or suspected ligatures that were found loose in the graves, can you exclude the possibility beyond medical or scientific certainty that they are not simply cloths used for identification in the manner that we have seen in these photographs from this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to 1D1148. This is another set of still photographs from a video. The video in question is the so-called Srebrenica trial video which is already in evidence. If it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last one we looked at was not included yet in the still that was admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The ones we looked at are all in the still that has been admitted into evidence. It's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also the ones we have not seen yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we were perhaps a bit premature. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Srebrenica trial video has footage of the survivors of the column of Bosnian Muslim men when they reached Tuzla and this image is taken from that 37 minutes and 37 seconds of that film. And we see that this individual who is -- who does not appear to be wearing a uniform but does have a rifle, has a loop of cloth around his neck and one around his head. And if we turn to the next page, I think we will see the other side of his body. And that shows the other view of his -- of the -- of the cloth around his head. Looking at these -- this photograph, can you exclude that -- can you exclude to a degree of scientific certainty that some of the ligatures and/or suspected blindfolds found in the graves might not in fact be this type of cloth used in the manner that this soldier -- pardon me, that the individual is using? And if you like, we can go back to the first picture.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can you show me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that some of the unassociated ligatures and blindfolds we see could be similar to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, perhaps you might not be able to know this without looking at your records, but do you recall if there were any instances where suspected blindfolds were found around the neck of a body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think we -- we found any of the -- that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- low down, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now in respect to the suspected ligatures, am I correct that for, I believe, four of the sites that you reviewed bodies from - that is to say, Petkovici Dam, Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4, Hodzici Road 5, and Zeleni Jadar, I guess that's five - there were either no ligatures or only one ligature located from those mass graves?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I've -- I just have to just check in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you want, we can go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's do it this way, sir. Petkovici Dam, am I correct that there was only one ligature recovered from that location?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hodzici Road 3, am I correct that there were no ligatures recovered from that location?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hodzici Road 4, am I correct only one ligature suspected was recovered from that location?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think on Hodzici 4 I listed it only as a possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exactly. And Hodzici Road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are we at this moment just repeating what is found in the report about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any specific reason to do that? Or would we just see what is in the report and then know how many were retrieved from the various graves?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's a fair comment, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would have one matter to be addressed. Is there agreement among the parties that the person being shown on this picture is carrying a hunting rifle and that he is without shoes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could even -- I think in the video it's -- I'd say it's a shot-gun, hunting rifle. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- details of the video available immediately. Then that seems to be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Should we tender -- this is the next Defence exhibit, Your Honour. I haven't tendered it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was unclear to me what was by the first series but this is now the second series.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit number D340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D340 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Lee, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. I only have two questions. May I please have P1532, and if we could go to page 7. If we could go to page 7? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lawrence, if you could take a look at the clothing worn by the people appearing in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And if we could please go to page 8. And now if we could go to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, you were asked questions about layers of clothes worn by the bodies that you examined. Is this -- are these the type of clothing consistent with the type of clothing that you've observed on the bodies that you examined?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Lawrence, you testified today about the bodies found in the Zeleni Jadar 5 grave-site. And if you were to learn or if you had known that the bodies found at Zeleni Jadar 5 were linked to the Kravica warehouse massacre and that hand grenades and other explosives were used in killing individuals -- those individuals, would the circumstances surrounding their death, would that be consistent with your findings, particularly concerning the high numbers of shrapnel injuries that were found on the bodies in that grave-site?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Lee. Mr. Lawrence, since the Chamber has no further questions for you either, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And as this is the last time I think I will attend, I would like to thank the ICTY staff for their courtesy and their help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They'll certainly appreciate this word of thanks. Whether it's the last time or not is not in the hands of this Chamber. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the suggestion was by the Prosecution that we would not call any further witnesses. There is only one thing I would like to briefly raise. The Chamber has expressed its intention to have a housekeeping session. The Chamber would prefer to do that on Thursday but wants to consult the parties, whether there is any objection to doing that. We do not think it will take the whole of the day but perhaps one and a half session looking at the list of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- MFIs. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to suit our schedule rather well, in fact. But if there is any issue, I will discuss it with the Defence, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- for the moment I would say that we are fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as matters stand now, Mr. Lukic, no problem to have it on Thursday? Then the Chamber schedules this housekeeping session on Thursday and we will consider, most likely on Wednesday, whether it will be in the beginning of the session or the second part of the morning session of Thursday, the 25th of July. We stand adjourned --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. We had one issue that we would like to address related to the evidentiary matter concerning RM506.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we would have to go into private session for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We adjourn for the day and will resume on Monday, the 22nd of July, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom III? Yes. Same courtroom III. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25
